lines.trans: Alisa, how do you like my restaurant?
Dad, look, do I look like you?
Of course, sunshine!
You have my eyes and smile.
And mom says something else.
She says, thank God, you do not look like him!
She was just joking.
Do not pay any attention.
Are you handsome too, Dad?
I am the most handsome chef in Moscow!
But mom says you are very funny.
Mom is simply jealous of my talent.
Then let us keep playing!
I am always ready to play with you.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: слава богу = thank God (literally 'glory to God')

examples.text: О, наконец тепло! Слава богу. Сейчас ещё чай сделаю.
examples.trans: Oh, it's warm at last! Thank goodness. Now I'll make some tea too.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Прошу внимания = May I have your attention
Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.note: 'закрывать глаза на' + accusative = to turn a blind eye to

examples.text: Я не буду закрывать на это глаза.
examples.trans: I'm not going to close my eyes to this.

examples.text: А я глаза на это закрывать не буду. Я подниму людей!
examples.trans: Well, I'm not going to close my eyes to this. I'll rally people!

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to speak, to talk') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
usually the short form: я готов (m), я готова (f)
давай + 1st person plural or infinitive
давай + 1st person plural or infinitive

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'next'.
Secondary conversational sense ('next, go on') (in a list or a story) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: А дальше? Я очень волнуюсь, я к этому не приспособлена.
examples.trans: And then what? I'm very nervous, I'm not cut out for this.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').
Secondary conversational sense ('different') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

завидовать.gloss: to envy, to be jealous of

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'видовать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to envy', forming an aspectual pair with 'позавидовать'.

examples.trans: I envy you in a good way.

examples.text: У него было ружьё. Все мальчишки завидовали ему.
examples.trans: He had an air gun. All the boys envied him.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: играть в + accusative (a game/sport)

examples.text: Напиши: трус не играет в хоккей.
examples.trans: Write: a coward doesn't play hockey.
The children are playing in the courtyard.

examples.text: Хорошая фотография! Напиши: трус не играет в хоккей.
examples.trans: Good photo! Write: a coward doesn't play hockey.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'team; command' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('command, order') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ничего страшного. Теперь мы одна команда.
examples.trans: Nothing serious. Now we're one team.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('beautiful, handsome').

examples.trans: They have a very beautiful house.

meanings.note: мам! = casual 'Mum!' when calling her
Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ращать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to turn, to direct', paired with 'обратить'.

examples.text: Не обращай внимания на его громкие шутки.
examples.trans: Do not pay attention to his loud jokes.

examples.text: Шеф всегда обращает внимание на каждую мелочь на тарелке.
examples.trans: The chef always pays attention to every little detail on the plate.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'личный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('excellent').

examples.text: Квартира будет отличная. На Симашко есть новый дом.
examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat. There's a new building on Simashko Street.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: declines like a feminine noun in -а, but is masculine

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: usually short form похож/похожа/похожи + на + accusative

examples.trans: He looks very much like his father.

examples.text: Нормально у вас тут, просторно. И маскировка хорошая, на дворников похожи.
examples.trans: It's nice in here, roomy. And good disguises—you look like janitors.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: forms the superlative: самый главный = the most important
Secondary conversational sense ('the very') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The most important thing is the people.
Do you know the main thing?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'glory', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('thank God') (in 'слава богу') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: О, наконец тепло! Слава богу. Сейчас ещё чай сделаю.
examples.trans: Oh, it's warm at last! Thank goodness. Now I'll make some tea too.

examples.text: Слава богу! Я пьяных за рулём просто терпеть не могу!
examples.trans: Thank goodness! I simply cannot stand drunk people behind the wheel!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мешной'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('funny, ridiculous').
Secondary conversational sense ('ridiculous, laughable') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты такой смешной, Тузик! Кто такой сладкий?
examples.trans: You're so funny, Tuzik! Who's so sweet?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look', forming an aspectual pair with 'посмотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch') (TV, a film) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'олнышко'). Common neuter noun meaning 'sweetheart, darling; little sun' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('little sun') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: In spring the warm sun shines.
Thank you, sweetheart. Go on, Yulya, work.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'talent', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: У этой девочки большой талант к музыке.
examples.trans: This girl has a great talent for music.

examples.text: Потому что твой папа прав! У тебя нет таланта.
examples.trans: Because your dad is right! You have no talent.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'too'.

examples.text: Мы же здесь выросли. И о людях тоже надо думать.
examples.trans: After all, we grew up here. And you have to think about people too.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'лыбка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'smile' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Все официанты готовы встречать гостей улыбкой.
examples.trans: All the waiters are ready to greet guests with a smile.

examples.text: У тебя мои глаза и улыбка.
examples.trans: You have my eyes and smile.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to joke', paired with 'пошутить'.

examples.text: Шутишь? Правда, скажи, где деньги? Меня наняли.
examples.trans: Are you joking? Seriously, tell me, where's the money? They hired me.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
